nyala.e: Probably borrowed from Tsonga nyala. The alternative form inyala is from Zulu inyala.

s.d: spiral-horned South African antelope with a fringe of white hairs along back and neck

A southern African antelope, Tragelaphus angasii (syn. Nyala angasii), with thin white stripes in the grey or brown coat, a ridge of tufted hair running all along the spine, and long horns with a spiral twist.
a small byte

nyctalopia.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νυκταλωπία (nuktalōpía), from νύξ (núx, “night”), ἀλαός (alaós, “blind”), and ὄψ (óps, “eye”).

s.d: inability to see clearly in dim light; due to a deficiency of vitamin A or to a retinal disorder
(uncountable) The inability to see clearly in dim light; night blindness

s.d: a morbid fear of night or darkness
excessive urination at night; especially common in older men

nylon.e: Coined by the company DuPont in 1938. According to the company, the name was formed from the random generic syllable nyl- + the common fiber suffix -on (as in rayon and Dacron), said to be ultimately from cotton.

s.d: a thermoplastic polyamide; a family of strong resilient synthetic fibers
a group of synthetic fabrics, known generically as aliphatic polyamides

(uncountable) Originally, the DuPont company trade name for polyamide, a copolymer whose molecules consist of alternating diamine and dicarboxylic acid monomers bonded together; now generically used for this type of polymer.
(uncountable) A stocking originally fabricated from nylon; also used generically for any long, sheer stocking worn on a woman's legs.
x: I tore a hole in my nylons while walking home through the woods.

1970-1975, Lou Sullivan, personal diary, quoted in 2019, Ellis Martin, Zach Ozma (editors), We Both Laughed In Pleasure
He put on make-up, nylons, panties, a dress.

s.d: (uncountable) A Queen's Counsel, King's Counsel or Senior Counsel who was appointed as a courtesy, rather than on merit.
women's stockings made from a sheer material (nylon or rayon or silk)
women's stockings made from a sheer material (nylon or rayon or silk)
(plural-only) stockings made from nylon
x: She sheathed her legs in the sheerest of the nylons that her father had brought back from the Continent, and slipped her feet into the toeless, high-heeled shoes of black suède.

nymph.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ-
Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē)der.
Latin nymphader.
Old French nimphebor.
Middle English nimphe
English nymph
From Middle English nimphe, from Old English nymphē and Old French nimphe, both from Latin nympha (“nymph, bride”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young maiden”). Doublet of nympha.

s.d: (classical mythology) a minor nature goddess usually depicted as a beautiful maiden
x: the ancient Greeks believed that nymphs inhabited forests and bodies of water

s.d: a larva of an insect with incomplete metamorphosis (as the dragonfly or mayfly)
a voluptuously beautiful young woman
Any female nature spirit associated with water, forests, grottos, wind, etc.
A young girl, especially one who is attractive, beautiful or graceful.
The larva of certain insects.
Any of various butterflies of the family Nymphalidae.
To fish using a nymph larva as bait.
x: Kuster meanwhile nymphed the middle of the Snag. When I joined him, I threw my streamer between the main channel's flow and the skinnier side-channel flow, […]

s.d: medium to large butterflies found worldwide typically having brightly colored wings and much-reduced nonfunctional forelegs carried folded on the breast
Any butterfly of the family Nymphalidae.
medium to large butterflies found worldwide typically having brightly colored wings and much-reduced nonfunctional forelegs carried folded on the breast

nymphet.e: From nymph + -et (“diminutive”), first attested 1612. The second sense was popularized by Vladimir Nabokov's 1955 novel Lolita.

s.d: a sexually attractive young woman
(obsolete) A small nymph.
x: Of the nymphets sporting there In Wyrrall, and in Delamere.

s.d: a woman with abnormal sexual desires
(derogatory, informal) A nymphomaniac.

nympholepsy.e: From nympho- + -lepsy, after Ancient Greek νυμφόληπτος (numphólēptos, “frenzied by the nymphs”, adjective).

s.d: a frenzy of emotion; as for something unattainable
(uncountable) A frenzied state of (usually erotic) emotion, especially concerning something or someone unattainable.
x: If young persons of both sexes were brought together in the honest practical relations of organized labor, we should see no more of these fond nympholepsies

s.d: (uncountable) Nymphophilia.
x: The science of nympholepsy is a precise science. Actual contact would do it in one second flat. An interspace of a millimeter would do it in ten.

nympholept.e: From Ancient Greek νυμφόληπτος (numphólēptos, “caught by nymphs, frenzied”), from νύμφη (númphē) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “I take”).

s.d: a person seized by nympholepsy

nymphomania.e: Borrowed from New Latin, from Latin nympha + -mania. By surface analysis, nympho- + mania.

s.d: abnormally intense sexual desire in women
(uncountable) Excess of sexual behaviour or desire in women.
x: Camphor, however, has been used to counteract the conditions arising from nymphomania.

nymphomaniac.e: From nymphomania + -ac. By surface analysis, nympho- + -maniac.

s.d: a woman with abnormal sexual desires
A woman who has an excessive libido.
x: Xenia's such a nymphomaniac that she's not even satisfied with three lovers.

s.d: (used of women) affected with excessive sexual desire
Of a woman, having an excessive libido.
(used of women) affected with excessive sexual desire
Characteristic of nymphomania or a nymphomaniac.

nystagmus.e: First attested in 1798. From New Latin nystagmus, from Ancient Greek νυσταγμός (nustagmós, “nodding, drowsiness”), from νυστάζω (nustázō, “nod, be sleepy”).

s.d: involuntary movements of the eyeballs; its presence or absence is used to diagnose a variety of neurological and visual disorders
(uncountable) Rapid and excessive involuntary eye movement, usually lateral.
x: For months Travis had seen his solitary figure, shoulders hunched inside the flying jacket, in more and more newsreels, as an extra in war films, and then as a patient in an elegant ophthalmic film on nystagmus
